Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**No Class May Be Certified Under Rule 23(b)(3) Because Individualized Damages Questions Will Overwhelm Any Common Ones.**

**A. Plaintiffs must prove predominance with evidence.**

Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that their proposed class satisfies Rule 23. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811 (7th Cir. 2012). Pleading the requirements is not enough. A court need not accept the complaint's allegations as true and must resolve the factual and legal disputes that bear on certification before certifying, even when they overlap with the merits. *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 675–77 (7th Cir. 2001).

Rule 23(b)(3)'s predominance criterion is more demanding than Rule 23(a)'s requirements. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34 (2013). Plaintiffs must show that damages can be measured on a classwide basis consistent with their theory of liability. *Id.* at 34–35. Without such a method, questions of individual damage calculations will inevitably overwhelm questions common to the class. *Id.* at 34. A promise to develop a method later does not carry that burden. *See Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–86 (7th Cir. 2014) (reversing certification where the district court did not adequately examine whether the plaintiffs' proposed proof, including proof of damages, could establish their claims classwide).

**B. Individualized damages proof would consume this litigation.**

*Espenscheid v. DirectSat USA, LLC*, 705 F.3d 770 (7th Cir. 2013), is instructive. There, technicians sought to litigate wage claims collectively although the amount of uncompensated time varied from worker to worker. *Id.* at 773–74. The plaintiffs proposed to rely on testimony from a subset of class members but did not show that the sample was representative or could reliably establish what others were owed. *Id.* at 774. Faced with the prospect of thousands of separate evidentiary hearings and no feasible trial plan, this Court affirmed decertification. *Id.* at 773–76.

The same defect is fatal here. Each member's recovery would turn on facts particular to that member: whether the member lost anything, how much, from what cause, and subject to what offsets or defenses. A damages model that averages away those differences would award money to some who suffered no loss and misstate what others are owed. Testing each claim would instead require a long series of individual trials, in which Defendant is entitled to contest each member's proof. Either way, the class device would not produce an efficient, reliable adjudication.

These problems are especially acute where individual inquiry is needed to decide not only the amount of damages but also whether Defendant is liable to a given member at all. *See Howland v. First Am. Title Ins. Co.*, 672 F.3d 525, 532–34 (7th Cir. 2012) (affirming denial of certification where liability required transaction-specific inquiry); *Harper v. Sheriff of Cook Cnty.*, 581 F.3d 511, 513–16 (7th Cir. 2009) (reversing certification where individualized issues predominated). A proposed class that sweeps in many people who suffered no injury compounds the difficulty. *See Oshana v. Coca-Cola Co.*, 472 F.3d 506, 513–14 (7th Cir. 2006) (affirming denial of certification where the proposed class could include millions who had no grievance).

**C. The rule permitting some damages variation does not save this class.**

Defendant does not contend that any variation in damages defeats certification. It does not. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815. Where a genuinely common liability question predominates, a court may resolve it classwide and leave damages to separate proceedings. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013). But that principle does not excuse Plaintiffs from showing predominance. It has no force where the individual inquiries are numerous, contested, and intertwined with injury and causation, such that a classwide ruling would leave the heart of each claim undecided. Nor may Plaintiffs defer the problem by invoking bifurcation or Rule 23(c)(4) without a concrete, workable plan for resolving what remains. *See Espenscheid*, 705 F.3d at 775–76. Certification under Rule 23(b)(3) should be denied.
